catalog_quote: It is necessary to include stress marking in an account of Eastern Tawbuid phonology since stress is contrastive in this language. Stress does not fall regularly on a particular syllable of the prosodic word, and it cannot be reliably predicted from other phonological properties of a word. Rather, stress is part of the underlying phonological representation of a word, and minimal pairs of words differentiated only by stress exist. Some examples are given here. (47) /sábi/ ‘basket’ /sabí/ ‘to slip off’ /balábaɡ/ ‘to obstruct a path’ /balabáɡ/ ‘morning’ /láman/ ‘so that’ /lamán/ ‘winnowing tray’ /sása/ ‘crushed rice grains’ /sasá/ ‘kind of wild banana’ ... new_statements.quote: It is necessary to include stress marking in an account of Eastern Tawbuid phonology since stress is contrastive in this language. Stress does not fall regularly on a particular syllable of the prosodic word, and it cannot be reliably predicted from other phonological properties of a word. Rather, stress is part of the underlying phonological representation of a word, and minimal pairs of words differentiated only by stress exist. [...] (p. 18:) All prosodic words must contain a primary stress; the same is not true for secondary stress. In production, primary stress can only fall on the ultimate or the penultimate syllable of a prosodic word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical/phonemic: each root (and some affixes) carries underlying stress marking, with minimal pairs such as /sábi/ 'basket' vs /sabí/ 'to slip off', /láman/ 'so that' vs /lamán/ 'winnowing tray'. Surface primary stress is confined to a two-syllable window at the right edge (final or penultimate syllable of the prosodic word), one primary stress per prosodic word. When suffixation pushes a stress-marked root syllable outside the window, primary stress goes to the final syllable (the suffix) and the root syllable surfaces with secondary stress ([tùl.bu.í] from /túlbu-i/); roots with final stress plus a suffix yield penultimate stress ([li.fú.ŋi]); inherently stressed suffixes such as -ún take the primary stress; roots ending in a closed syllable with /a/ always surface with penultimate stress when suffixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Two levels, primary (acute) and secondary (grave). Secondary stress is also contrastive on some affixes (prefix /bà-/ 'smelling of' vs /ba-/ acquisition: /bàujáŋ/ 'smelling of fish' vs /baujáŋ/ 'fish that someone has acquired', p. 17) and arises when a stress-marked root syllable ends up antepenultimate under suffixation; secondary stress is not restricted to the final two syllables and is not obligatory.
new_statements.exceptions: Intonation can override lexical stress (e.g. a scolding contour makes the phrase-penultimate syllable phonetically stressed regardless of marking, fn. 11 p. 19); roots with a closed final syllable containing /a/ (e.g. /tarábaŋ/) take penultimate stress in all suffixed forms regardless of marking (p. 20); a few other rare phonologically conditioned exceptions are mentioned but not described (fn. 15); stressed vowels may be longer, vowel length itself not contrastive (p. 13).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (root plus affixes; clitic/word-boundary processes discussed in 2.6). Statements are based on elicited words and recorded texts from Safa village (Oriental Mindoro), with two sound-file illustrations of stressed syllables (loudness, duration). Author notes phonetic stress does not map one-to-one onto phonemic stress marking because of the final/penult window, stressed suffixes and intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Fleming 2022 describes Eastern Tawbuid [bnj] = east2482 exactly (author states the ISO code), based on fieldwork in Safa village, Oriental Mindoro (12°58'45''N 121°19'40''E), a Christianised Eastern Tawbuid community on the edge of the Tawbuid area. The Wikipedia stress paragraph ('final or penultimate, mostly unpredictable') is placed under Western Tawbuid [twb] = west2559 and is unsourced; the Zorc 'Taubuid (Batangan)' notes are also mainly Western Tawbuid.
